entry.title: [djust] djust: Arbitrary absolute-path file read in the find_handlers_for_template MCP tool
entry.content:
Affected version / file / line

Version: djust v1.1.4 (latest release, published 2026-09-23). File: python/djust/mcp/server.py:354-433 (MCP tool find_handlers_for_template). Confirmed identical on the commit used for triage, a7e4fafd1667b4db0b1465652d4a63cb17117a07.

Description

@mcp.tool()
def find_handlers_for_template(template_path: str) -> str:
    """
    Args:
        template_path: Either a logical template name (e.g.
            'demos/counter.html' — what you'd pass to `render`) OR
            an absolute filesystem path. Both are searched.
    """
    ...
    resolved_path: str | None = None
    if os.path.isabs(template_path) and os.path.isfile(template_path):
        resolved_path = template_path
    else:
        ...  # logical-name resolution via Django's template loader
    ...
    with open(resolved_path, "r", encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as f:
        source = f.read()
    handler_names_in_template = sorted({m.group(2) for m in dj_event_attr_re.finditer(source)})

When template_path is an absolute path to an existing file, it is used directly, with no confinement to the project/template directories — no realpath() + prefix check, no allowlist. open(resolved_path, ...) then reads the file.

This is inconsistent with the sibling tool in the same file (loaddata, ~line 290-303), which explicitly rejects paths outside the project directory for its own path-like parameter:

candidate = os.path.realpath(...)
if base_dir and not candidate.startswith(os.path.realpath(str(base_dir))):
    return json.dumps({"error": f"fixture path '{p}' resolves outside the project directory", ...})

find_handlers_for_template has no equivalent check for template_path before the open() call.

Impact

An MCP client with access to this tool (available whenever the Django project is running the MCP server via python manage.py djust_mcp — no separate opt-in flag gates this specific tool beyond that) can read the contents of any file on disk that the process has read permission to and that exists, by passing an absolute path — e.g. /etc/passwd, application .env files, SSH keys, or any other sensitive file reachable by the server process's user.

Mitigating factor (reduces this from High to Medium): the tool does not return the raw file content. It runs one fixed regex (dj-(?:click|submit|change|input|keydown|keyup)\s*=\s*'"['"]) against the content and returns only the matched handler-name strings, plus confirmation that the file exists and is readable (an existence/readability oracle on its own, independent of the regex match). If the targeted file happens to contain text matching that HTML-attribute-like pattern (plausible for config files, logs, or any text file with key="value"-shaped content), those substrings are returned in full — so the read is not purely blind, but it is not a general-purpose arbitrary-file-read primitive either.

Proof of Concept / Reproduction Traced via direct source read; no live Django project was exercised for this report (would require a full djust project scaffold, which was out of scope for this pass — see limitation below).

  1. MCP client calls: find_handlers_for_template(template_path="/etc/passwd")
  2. server.py ~line 393:
       if os.path.isabs(template_path) and os.path.isfile(template_path):
       resolved_path = template_path
    resolved_path == "/etc/passwd", unchanged, unconfined
  3. server.py ~line 430:
       with open(resolved_path, "r", encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as f:
       source = f.read()
    /etc/passwd is now fully read into source
  4. The regex dj_event_attr_re.finditer(source) is applied to the real /etc/passwd content. /etc/passwd will not match this specific pattern, so the response would report an empty handler list plus "file exists and was read" - which already confirms the path-confinement bypass (compare with passing a nonexistent absolute path, which correctly returns "Template file not found").
  5. On a target where the absolute path points to a file that DOES contain text shaped like dj-click="..." (e.g. a copied HTML fragment, a stray config value, or a crafted file placed by the attacker via another vector), the matched substrings are returned verbatim in the JSON response - full-content disclosure of just those substrings, not the whole file.

Suggested Fix

Apply the same confinement loaddata already uses, before the os.path.isfile check:

if os.path.isabs(template_path):
    candidate = os.path.realpath(template_path)
    if base_dir and not candidate.startswith(os.path.realpath(str(base_dir))):
        return json.dumps({
            "error": f"template path '{template_path}' resolves outside the project directory",
            "resolved": candidate,
            "project_dir": str(base_dir),
        })
    if os.path.isfile(candidate):
        resolved_path = candidate

Limitations

Not exercised against a live Django/djust project — this is a source-level trace of the exact executed branch (os.path.isabs + os.path.isfile + open()), not an end-to-end runtime capture. Did not verify whether any MCP-host-level confirmation/approval step (some MCP clients prompt the user before a tool call with a suspicious-looking path argument) would intercept this in practice - the vulnerability is in the server's own missing server-side guard regardless of client-side UX.

Disclosure Timeline

2026-09-24: found during audit, confirmed via source trace to the open() sink; classified Medium due to the response-content limitation (matched substrings only, not raw file content). Please check the log file, and apply CVE once the fix is made.

10  14:53:20.187205 write(1, "{\"error\": \"Could not resolve tem"..., 204) = 204
   ...
10  14:53:20.191831 write(1, "=== ATTACK: absolute path OUTSID"..., 57) = 57
10  14:53:20.194864 write(1, "target path:", 12) = 12
10  14:53:20.198521 write(1, "/case/outside/evil_content.html", 31) = 31

Maintainer assessment

The djust MCP server (manage.py djust_mcp, python -m djust.mcp) only serves stdio to the MCP client that launched it, as the same OS user, on the developer's machine; there is no network listener. The realistic caller is a local AI agent acting on untrusted input. The tool returns only dj-*-attribute-shaped substrings and an existence answer, not file contents. We therefore rate this Low (CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N, 3.3).

The seed_fixtures guard compared paths with a string prefix (so /app-data passed for a BASE_DIR of /app) and skipped the check when BASE_DIR was unset; it now compares whole path components and refuses without BASE_DIR. Both use one containment helper.

entry.title: [djust] djust: Arbitrary absolute-path file read in the find_handlers_for_template MCP tool
entry.content:
Affected version / file / line

Version: djust v1.1.4 (latest release, published 2026-09-23). File: python/djust/mcp/server.py:354-433 (MCP tool find_handlers_for_template). Confirmed identical on the commit used for triage, a7e4fafd1667b4db0b1465652d4a63cb17117a07.

Description

@mcp.tool()
def find_handlers_for_template(template_path: str) -> str:
    """
    Args:
        template_path: Either a logical template name (e.g.
            'demos/counter.html' — what you'd pass to `render`) OR
            an absolute filesystem path. Both are searched.
    """
    ...
    resolved_path: str | None = None
    if os.path.isabs(template_path) and os.path.isfile(template_path):
        resolved_path = template_path
    else:
        ...  # logical-name resolution via Django's template loader
    ...
    with open(resolved_path, "r", encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as f:
        source = f.read()
    handler_names_in_template = sorted({m.group(2) for m in dj_event_attr_re.finditer(source)})

When template_path is an absolute path to an existing file, it is used directly, with no confinement to the project/template directories — no realpath() + prefix check, no allowlist. open(resolved_path, ...) then reads the file.

This is inconsistent with the sibling tool in the same file (loaddata, ~line 290-303), which explicitly rejects paths outside the project directory for its own path-like parameter:

candidate = os.path.realpath(...)
if base_dir and not candidate.startswith(os.path.realpath(str(base_dir))):
    return json.dumps({"error": f"fixture path '{p}' resolves outside the project directory", ...})

find_handlers_for_template has no equivalent check for template_path before the open() call.

Impact

An MCP client with access to this tool (available whenever the Django project is running the MCP server via python manage.py djust_mcp — no separate opt-in flag gates this specific tool beyond that) can read the contents of any file on disk that the process has read permission to and that exists, by passing an absolute path — e.g. /etc/passwd, application .env files, SSH keys, or any other sensitive file reachable by the server process's user.

Mitigating factor (reduces this from High to Medium): the tool does not return the raw file content. It runs one fixed regex (dj-(?:click|submit|change|input|keydown|keyup)\s*=\s*'"['"]) against the content and returns only the matched handler-name strings, plus confirmation that the file exists and is readable (an existence/readability oracle on its own, independent of the regex match). If the targeted file happens to contain text matching that HTML-attribute-like pattern (plausible for config files, logs, or any text file with key="value"-shaped content), those substrings are returned in full — so the read is not purely blind, but it is not a general-purpose arbitrary-file-read primitive either.

Proof of Concept / Reproduction Traced via direct source read; no live Django project was exercised for this report (would require a full djust project scaffold, which was out of scope for this pass — see limitation below).

  1. MCP client calls: find_handlers_for_template(template_path="/etc/passwd")
  2. server.py ~line 393:
       if os.path.isabs(template_path) and os.path.isfile(template_path):
       resolved_path = template_path
    resolved_path == "/etc/passwd", unchanged, unconfined
  3. server.py ~line 430:
       with open(resolved_path, "r", encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as f:
       source = f.read()
    /etc/passwd is now fully read into source
  4. The regex dj_event_attr_re.finditer(source) is applied to the real /etc/passwd content. /etc/passwd will not match this specific pattern, so the response would report an empty handler list plus "file exists and was read" - which already confirms the path-confinement bypass (compare with passing a nonexistent absolute path, which correctly returns "Template file not found").
  5. On a target where the absolute path points to a file that DOES contain text shaped like dj-click="..." (e.g. a copied HTML fragment, a stray config value, or a crafted file placed by the attacker via another vector), the matched substrings are returned verbatim in the JSON response - full-content disclosure of just those substrings, not the whole file.

Suggested Fix

Apply the same confinement loaddata already uses, before the os.path.isfile check:

if os.path.isabs(template_path):
    candidate = os.path.realpath(template_path)
    if base_dir and not candidate.startswith(os.path.realpath(str(base_dir))):
        return json.dumps({
            "error": f"template path '{template_path}' resolves outside the project directory",
            "resolved": candidate,
            "project_dir": str(base_dir),
        })
    if os.path.isfile(candidate):
        resolved_path = candidate

Limitations

Not exercised against a live Django/djust project — this is a source-level trace of the exact executed branch (os.path.isabs + os.path.isfile + open()), not an end-to-end runtime capture. Did not verify whether any MCP-host-level confirmation/approval step (some MCP clients prompt the user before a tool call with a suspicious-looking path argument) would intercept this in practice - the vulnerability is in the server's own missing server-side guard regardless of client-side UX.

entry.title: [virtualenv] virtualenv bash activate runs commands from an environment name with a backslash before $
entry.content:
Summary

The bash activate script escapes the environment name for only one of the two passes bash makes over PS1, so a backslash in the name undoes the escaping and a name containing \$(...) runs as commands in the user's shell each time bash draws the prompt.

Affected area

src/virtualenv/activation/bash/activate.sh, the block that prepends the environment name to PS1.

Attacker-controlled input

The environment name: the environment directory's name, or the --prompt or VIRTUALENV_PROMPT value. An attacker needs to influence it, for example through a CI job or wrapper tool that passes a branch, project or job name through, or a directory in a cloned repository or unpacked archive. --prompt . takes the current directory's name.

Details

bash handles PS1 in two passes each time it draws the prompt: it first decodes backslash prompt escapes, turning \\ into \ and \$ into $ (or # for root), and then runs parameter expansion, command substitution and arithmetic expansion on the result. Since 21.13.0 the script escapes backslashes, dollar signs and backticks in the name, but only for the second pass, so the decode pass strips the escaping that a backslash in the name precedes. Releases before 21.13.0 do not escape the name at all. A bash running as root decodes \$ to #, so the payload shows the wrong text there but runs nothing. zsh does no decode pass and is not affected.

Proof of concept

$ virtualenv --prompt 'a\$(touch PWNED)' env
$ bash --norc --noprofile -c 'source env/bin/activate; printf "%s" "${PS1@P}"'
$ ls PWNED
PWNED

Impact

Arbitrary command execution in the shell of a user who sources the activate script of an environment whose name an attacker influenced, with that user's privileges, once per prompt draw.

Versions tested

21.14.6 with bash 5.2.15 on Debian bookworm, as an unprivileged user and as root.

Known mitigation

Set VIRTUAL_ENV_DISABLE_PROMPT=1 before you source activate, which leaves PS1 alone, or run shopt -u promptvars if your prompt does not need expansion. Check the name of an environment you did not create before you source its activate.

Latest release

  • The problem reproduces on the latest virtualenv release.

21.14.6

Patches

Fixed in 21.14.7. Under bash, activate now escapes backslashes, dollar signs and backticks for both passes, so the example above runs nothing and the prompt shows the name as given. zsh keeps the single escaping it needs. Fix: https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/commit/c3104e02474b652832a9bbaae79f6e1696296932

Credits

Found while running the virtualenv test suite as root inside the Anthropic OSS Scanner build image.

entry.title: [virtualenv] virtualenv activate runs commands from the environment name in zsh with PROMPT_SUBST
entry.content:
Impact

zsh users activate an environment with the bash activate script, which puts the environment name into PS1. Since 21.13.0 the script escapes backslashes, dollar signs and backticks in that name, but only when BASH_VERSION is set, so zsh gets the raw value. With the PROMPT_SUBST option set, zsh runs parameter expansion, command substitution and arithmetic expansion on PS1 each time it draws the prompt. A name that contains $(...), backticks or ${...} then runs as commands in the user's shell, once per prompt.

The name comes from the environment directory, or from --prompt or VIRTUALENV_PROMPT. After you create an environment with:

$ virtualenv 'x$(touch PWNED)y'

source 'x$(touch PWNED)y/bin/activate' in a zsh session with PROMPT_SUBST set creates PWNED, and the prompt shows (xy). Passing that value as --prompt to an environment with a plain name has the same effect. Without PROMPT_SUBST, zsh shows the name as text and runs nothing. bash runs nothing either.

A plain zsh starts with PROMPT_SUBST off. oh-my-zsh users have it on: oh-my-zsh loads lib/theme-and-appearance.zsh at startup, and that file sets it. An attacker needs to influence the environment path or prompt: a CI job or wrapper tool that passes a branch, project or job name through, or a directory in a cloned repository or unpacked archive. --prompt . takes the current directory's name.

zsh also reads % in PS1 as a prompt escape, so a name with %n showed the user name in place of those characters, though without running commands.

The bug is in releases up to and including 21.14.3. The payload runs on 20.26.6 and 21.14.3, and the reporter confirmed 21.9.1.

Patches

Fixed in 21.14.4. Under zsh, activate now escapes the name the way it does under bash and doubles %, so the example above runs nothing and the prompt shows the name as given. zsh gets the escaping even when PROMPT_SUBST is off, because a user can set the option after activation; a name with a backslash, dollar sign or backtick then shows the added backslashes. Fix: https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/commit/5b915367da82bd024b2a0d28d2f98007034b4aa2

Workarounds

Set VIRTUAL_ENV_DISABLE_PROMPT=1 before you source activate, which leaves PS1 alone, or run unsetopt prompt_subst if your prompt does not need it. Check the name of an environment you did not create before you source its activate.

Credits

Kaya Emre Arikan (@kemrec) reported this issue.

entry.title: [virtualenv] virtualenv activate.fish runs commands from a path or prompt with a backslash before a quote
entry.content:
Impact

FishActivator defines no quote(), so it inherits ViaTemplateActivator.quote, which returns shlex.quote(string). That function follows POSIX sh rules, where a backslash inside single quotes stays a literal character. fish reads \' inside single quotes as an escaped quote and \\ as an escaped backslash. A value with a backslash before a quote therefore ends the literal somewhere other than where shlex.quote put the end, and fish expands the command substitution that follows.

The environment path reaches set -gx VIRTUAL_ENV, and --prompt or VIRTUALENV_PROMPT reaches set -gx VIRTUAL_ENV_PROMPT. For --prompt "x\'\$(touch PWNED)'\'", the generated activate.fish contains:

set -gx VIRTUAL_ENV_PROMPT 'x\'"'"'$(touch PWNED)'"'"'\'"'"''

source bin/activate.fish runs touch PWNED, and fish prints no error. The same payload as a directory name runs through VIRTUAL_ENV. --prompt . takes the current directory's name, so running virtualenv inside a directory someone else named is enough. Without the backslash the payload runs nothing, and under bash it runs nothing either.

virtualenv generates activate.fish by default. An attacker needs to influence the environment path or prompt: a CI job or wrapper tool that passes a branch, project or job name through, or a directory in a cloned repository or unpacked archive.

The bug affects every release up to 21.14.1 that ships activate.fish. The GHSA-p58f-9548-mpm2 fix in 21.7.13 moved the placeholders outside their quotes but kept shlex.quote.

Patches

Fixed in 21.14.2. activate.fish now escapes backslashes and single quotes the way fish reads them, so the example above runs nothing and shows the prompt as given. Fix: https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/commit/3bddeaf8d02c3ee7f576503efb082f8f494cfcab

Workarounds

Do not create an environment whose path or prompt contains a backslash, and inspect activate.fish before you source one you did not create.

Credits

Kevin Stubbings (@Kwstubbs) of GitHub Security Lab reported this issue.

entry.title: [virtualenv] virtualenv activation scripts run code from a path that contains a placeholder name
entry.content:
Impact

ViaTemplateActivator.instantiate_template replaces the placeholders in an activation template one key at a time, each across the whole text. When a value that it already substituted and quoted contains the name of a later placeholder, the later pass rewrites that name inside the quoted literal. The inserted value brings its own quotes, which close the outer literal, and the rest of the path runs as code when a user activates the environment.

__VIRTUAL_NAME__ holds the environment's directory name, so a destination such as A__VIRTUAL_NAME__B/x'$(touch PWNED)'y is enough. In the default activate for bash, the VIRTUAL_ENV line renders as:

VIRTUAL_ENV='/tmp/t/A'x'"'"'$(touch PWNED)'"'"'y'B/x'"'"'$(touch PWNED)'"'"'y'

Sourcing that script runs touch PWNED. The same payload in a path without the placeholder name runs nothing. activate.fish runs the command the same way, and the reporter also showed Python code execution through activate.xsh and bin/activate_this.py. In activate.csh, a directory named after a prompt display placeholder, such as __VIRTUAL_PROMPT_DISPLAY_TCSH__, breaks the script with Unmatched '''.

No change to quote() can stop this, because the rewrite happens after quote() ran; it defeats shlex.quote and repr() alike.

An attacker needs to influence the destination path or --prompt: a CI job or wrapper tool that builds the path from a branch or project name, or a directory in a cloned repository or unpacked archive.

The bug affects versions 20.26.6 through 21.14.1. Version 20.26.6 first quoted template values (#2768) and introduced the per-key loop.

Patches

Fixed in 21.14.2. Activation scripts now keep a placeholder name in the environment's path or prompt as plain text, and activating the example above runs nothing. Fix: https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/commit/602b26623a724827ff171bf11fef4ad186d01f74

Workarounds

Do not create an environment whose path or --prompt contains a placeholder name such as __VIRTUAL_NAME__, __VIRTUAL_ENV__ or __VIRTUAL_PROMPT__, and inspect the generated activation script before you source one you did not create.

entry.title: [Pillow] Pillow: Out-of-bounds access in _imagingmorph on a zero-width image
entry.content:
Summary

A PPM or PGM file can declare a width of 0, which Pillow accepts, producing an image of size (0, N). Passing that image to ImageMorph.MorphOp.apply() makes the native morphology code index a row buffer at outrow[width - 1], which is outrow[-1] when the width is 0. The process crashes.

Details

The PPM parser reads width and height with no lower-bound check:

  • src/PIL/PpmImagePlugin.py:119

The native apply() writes the row edges with no guard that the width is positive:

  • src/_imagingmorph.c:81 sets outrow[0] = outrow[width - 1] = 0;

match() and get_on_pixels() use the same edge-indexing pattern.

PoC

from PIL import Image, ImageMorph

# A width-0 image (also producible from a crafted PPM header). apply() indexes
# outrow[width - 1] == outrow[-1] in native code.
im = Image.new("L", (0, 5))
ImageMorph.MorphOp(op_name="dilation4").apply(im)

Run it:

$ python 03_poc.py
Segmentation fault (core dumped)

Observed on a source build of commit 3e2ab96.

Under AddressSanitizer:

==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address (pc ... in apply)
    #0 apply   src/_imagingmorph.c:81
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: SEGV src/_imagingmorph.c:81 in apply

With width 0 the outrow[width - 1] write lands on an unmapped page, so it surfaces as a SEGV pinned to the edge-write line rather than a redzone overflow.

Impact

Out-of-bounds write in a C extension. Affects any application that runs a morphology operation on an image opened from untrusted input. Result is a crash and possible memory corruption.

References

  • https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/security/advisories/GHSA-58r4-6rv3-gfh8
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-112397
  • https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/commit/18f7c0dfee93063c51db6ed0ca8c4da2999dcb64

entry.title: [Pillow] Pillow: GIF seek keeps rejected size after DecompressionBombError, allowing DoS
entry.content:
============================================================================
GIF seek keeps rejected size after DecompressionBombError, allowing DoS
Location: src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:293  in GifImageFile._seek()
Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6
============================================================================

A GIF of about 60 bytes can make Pillow allocate gigabytes of memory. This affects applications that catch the "image too large" error raised while stepping to a later animation frame and then keep using the same image object. Pillow correctly refuses the oversized frame, but it stores the refused dimensions on the image object anyway, and later operations size their memory from them. An attacker who can upload a GIF to such a service can exhaust its memory: the process either fails with an out-of-memory error after committing gigabytes, or is killed by the operating system. There is no memory corruption.

The bug is in GifImageFile._seek() (src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:292-294). When a frame's extent enlarges the image, the code assigns the new size to self._size and only then calls Image._decompression_bomb_check(). Nothing restores the old size when DecompressionBombError is raised, because seek() only rolls back on EOFError. After the caught error, im.size reports the rejected size while the pixel buffer im.im is still the 1×1 first frame. Because the extent is a 16-bit offset plus a 16-bit size, that rejected size can be as large as 131070×131070.

In the attached reproducer, the rejected size is 40000×40000. A retried seek(1) followed by load() then reaches load_prepare(), which calls Image.core.fill() with that size to decode a single pixel. Peak memory rises from 17 MiB to 1700 MiB before a 3 GiB address-space cap stops the next allocation. Image.new("RGB", im.size, ...) and rotate(..., expand=True) also allocate from the stale size.

The default paths are unaffected: plain Image.open() plus load(), ImageSequence.Iterator, and n_frames/is_animated. The ordering was introduced in c9f1b35e9810 ("Added GIF decompression bomb check", 2022-06-30, first released in 9.2.0), the check added for CVE-2022-45198. The two dispose-extent checks later in the same function already validate before using the size, and the attached patch makes this check follow the same order.

Details

GifImageFile._seek() lets a later frame enlarge the image, and performs the decompression-bomb check for the new size only after storing it on the object:

# src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:289-294  (GifImageFile._seek)
x0, y0 = i16(s, 0), i16(s, 2)
x1, y1 = x0 + i16(s, 4), y0 + i16(s, 6)
if (x1 > self.size[0] or y1 > self.size[1]) and update_image:
    self._size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1])   # state mutated
    Image._decompression_bomb_check(self._size)                 # ...then validated

_decompression_bomb_check() (src/PIL/Image.py:3586) raises DecompressionBombError for anything above 2 * MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS (178 956 970 px by default), but by then self._size already holds the rejected value and nothing restores it: seek() (GifImagePlugin.py:166-179) only rolls back on EOFError, and _seek(0) only ever grows _size. The object that the application still holds therefore reports im.size == (40000, 40000) while im.im is the 1×1 buffer of frame 0. Compare the two dispose-extent checks a few lines further down in the same function (GifImagePlugin.py:383 and :407), which call _decompression_bomb_check(dispose_size) before the corresponding Image.core.fill(), and TiffImagePlugin.load_prepare() (src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1319-1321), which checks _tile_size before allocating from it.

With this 60-byte GIF (hex)

47494638396101000100800000000000ffffff          GIF89a, 1x1 screen, 2-entry global palette
2c000000000100010000 02 024401 00               frame 0: 1x1 @ (0,0), LZW data
2c00000000409c409c00                            frame 1 descriptor: 40000x40000 @ (0,0)
2c000000000100010000 02 024401 00               another 1x1 frame
3b                                              trailer

Image.open() succeeds (im.size == (1, 1)), im.seek(1) raises DecompressionBombError: Image size (1600000000 pixels) exceeds limit of 178956970 pixels, and afterwards im.size == (40000, 40000), im.im.size == (1, 1), im.tell() == 0.

What happens next depends on what the application does with the object, but several ordinary operations take their dimensions from im.size rather than from the C buffer:

  • Retrying im.seek(1). The failed _seek left self.__offset == 0 and the file pointer just past the 9-byte descriptor, so the retry parses whatever follows — in the file above, a valid 1×1 frame — and succeeds. im.load() then runs GifImageFile.load_prepare():
    # src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:452-456
elif self.mode in ("RGB", "RGBA"):
    self._prev_im = self.im
    if self._frame_palette:
        self.im = Image.core.fill("P", self.size, self._frame_transparency or 0)
    which allocates and memsets a 40000×40000 "P" image (1.6 GB) to decode a 1×1 tile into, and load_end() (GifImagePlugin.py:485-491) fills a second one and converts it to RGB (another 1.6 GB + 6.4 GB).
  • im.rotate(angle, expand=True) for a non-multiple-of-90 angle, or the common flatten-onto-background idiom Image.new("RGB", im.size, bg), allocate from im.size as well (measured on an object poisoned to 20000×20000: rotate(45, expand=True) completes and touches 776 MiB; Image.new("RGB", im.size, "white") touches 1.5 GiB). Operations that pass im.size as a box against the real buffer (thumbnail, resize, save) fail with ValueError/SystemError instead.

The extent fields are 16-bit offset plus 16-bit size, so the stored size can be pushed to 131070×131070 (17.2 Gpx; 17 GB for mode "P", 69 GB for "RGB"/"RGBA" storage), 96× the error threshold.

n_frames / is_animated are not affected: they call _seek(frame, update_image=False), which skips the _size assignment (the file above reports n_frames == 2, is_animated == True and leaves im.size at 1×1).

Impact

A remote user who can upload a GIF to a service that (a) seeks animation frames and (b) catches the exception from seek() — a broad except Exception around a while True: im.seek(im.tell()+1) frame-collection loop, or an explicit except DecompressionBombError: log and continue — and then keeps using the same Image object, ends up driving allocations of 1.6 GB to tens of GB from a 60-byte file: MemoryError after the process has committed gigabytes, or an OOM kill of the worker when no address-space limit is set. The MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS guard fires, but does not actually keep the rejected dimensions out of the object it is guarding.

The precondition is real application behaviour but not the default path: Image.open(); im.load() is unaffected, and ImageSequence.Iterator propagates the error out of the for statement (a try inside the loop body does not swallow it). Hence low severity. This is adjacent to the GIF extent bomb check added for CVE-2022-45198: the ordering was introduced with that check in c9f1b35e9810 ("Added GIF decompression bomb check", 2022-06-30), first released in Pillow 9.2.0. Before it, the same size growth happened with no check at all; the check introduced there is the one that runs too late.

Reproducing

repro is a single Python script run against the installed Pillow. It needs about 1.7 GB of free RAM.

  1. setup_env() caps the process address space at 3 GiB with RLIMIT_AS, so the oversized allocations end in MemoryError instead of the OOM killer. It then opens the 60-byte GIF shown above, built in memory by bomb_gif(). The GIF contains a 1×1 screen and a 1×1 frame 0, so Image.open() passes its own bomb check. Next comes a bare frame-1 image descriptor that declares 40000×40000 (1.6 Gpx, about 9× the error threshold). A real 1×1 frame follows it.
  2. poc() calls im.seek(1) and catches DecompressionBombError, the way an application that skips bad frames would.
  3. First check: the state is inconsistent. The script prints im.size next to the real pixel buffer im.im.size. If the rejected frame had left the object unchanged, both would be (1, 1). On the affected code im.size is (40000, 40000).
  4. Second check: memory use. The script retries im.seek(1), which now parses the trailing 1×1 frame, and calls im.load(). It prints the process's peak RSS before and after. load_prepare() sizes its Image.core.fill() from im.size, so loading a single pixel fills a 1.6 GB buffer before the 3 GiB cap stops the next allocation.

Expected output on the affected tree:

open(): 60-byte GIF, size=(1, 1)
seek(1) raised as intended: Image size (1600000000 pixels) exceeds limit of 178956970 pixels, could be decompression bomb DOS attack.
after the caught error: im.size=(40000, 40000), pixel buffer im.im.size=(1, 1)
seek(1) + load() of a 1x1 frame: MemoryError at the 3 GiB cap; peak RSS 18 MiB -> 1700 MiB
BUG

The script prints BUG only if both checks hold: the over-limit size stayed on the object after the exception, and peak RSS grew by more than 1000 MiB while loading a 1×1 frame. Otherwise it prints OK. With the attached patch applied, it prints im.size=(1, 1), peak RSS stays at about 23 MiB, and the last line is OK.

Suggested fix

The attached patch validates before mutating in GifImageFile._seek() (src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:292-294): the enlarged extent is computed into a local, passed to _decompression_bomb_check(), and only then assigned to self._size, matching the order of the two dispose_size checks further down the same function. A rejected frame therefore leaves the object in its pre-seek state; valid files behave as before, and the exception is still raised at the same point:

--- a/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py
+++ b/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py
@@ -290,8 +290,9 @@ class GifImageFile(ImageFile.ImageFile):
                 x0, y0 = i16(s, 0), i16(s, 2)
                 x1, y1 = x0 + i16(s, 4), y0 + i16(s, 6)
                 if (x1 > self.size[0] or y1 > self.size[1]) and update_image:
-                    self._size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1])
-                    Image._decompression_bomb_check(self._size)
+                    size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1])
+                    Image._decompression_bomb_check(size)
+                    self._size = size
                 frame_dispose_extent = x0, y0, x1, y1
                 flags = s[8]

n_frames / is_animated go through update_image=False and are unaffected. The patch also extends test_exception_gif_extents in Tests/test_decompression_bomb.py to assert that im.size is unchanged after the DecompressionBombError. It does not change seek() itself; optionally, seek() could also treat DecompressionBombError like EOFError and re-seek to last_frame, so that a retried seek() does not resume parsing from the middle of the rejected frame.

The patch

GIF: run the decompression bomb check on an enlarging frame's extent before storing it in self._size

Applies to src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py at the commit above.

diff --git a/Tests/test_decompression_bomb.py b/Tests/test_decompression_bomb.py
index 98d833736..83cc785fc 100644
--- a/Tests/test_decompression_bomb.py
+++ b/Tests/test_decompression_bomb.py
@@ -63,6 +63,9 @@ class TestDecompressionBomb:
             with pytest.raises(Image.DecompressionBombError):
                 im.seek(1)
 
+            # The rejected frame should not have changed the image size
+            assert im.size == (100, 100)
+
     def test_exception_gif_zero_width(self, monkeypatch: pytest.MonkeyPatch) -> None:
         # Set limit to trigger exception on the test file
         monkeypatch.setattr(Image, "MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS", 4 * 64 * 128)
diff --git a/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py
index 11fb180fc..f9bda06c2 100644
--- a/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py
+++ b/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py
@@ -290,8 +290,9 @@ class GifImageFile(ImageFile.ImageFile):
                 x0, y0 = i16(s, 0), i16(s, 2)
                 x1, y1 = x0 + i16(s, 4), y0 + i16(s, 6)
                 if (x1 > self.size[0] or y1 > self.size[1]) and update_image:
-                    self._size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1])
-                    Image._decompression_bomb_check(self._size)
+                    size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1])
+                    Image._decompression_bomb_check(size)
+                    self._size = size
                 frame_dispose_extent = x0, y0, x1, y1
                 flags = s[8]

The reproducer

Reproducer — repro, 2,474 bytes (click to open)

Its last line is BUG when the issue triggers and OK when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed BUG.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# GifImageFile._seek() stores a frame's enlarged size in self._size and only
# *then* runs the decompression-bomb check. The check raises, but the object
# keeps the rejected 40000x40000 size over its real 1x1 pixel buffer, and the
# next load() allocates from that size: 1.6+ GB for a 60-byte GIF.
import io
import resource
import struct

from PIL import Image

BOMB = 40000  # 40000x40000 = 1.6 Gpx, ~9x the DecompressionBombError threshold
LIMIT = 2 * Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS


def frame_1x1():
    # image descriptor at (0,0) 1x1, then a 1-pixel LZW stream
    return b"," + struct.pack("<HHHHB", 0, 0, 1, 1, 0) + b"\x02\x02\x44\x01\x00"


def bomb_gif():
    return (
        b"GIF89a" + struct.pack("<HHBBB", 1, 1, 0x80, 0, 0) + b"\x00" * 3 + b"\xff" * 3
        + frame_1x1()                                         # frame 0: 1x1, passes open()
        + b"," + struct.pack("<HHHHB", 0, 0, BOMB, BOMB, 0)   # frame 1 claims 40000x40000
        + frame_1x1()                                         # a real 1x1 frame follows
        + b";"
    )


def peak_rss_mib():
    return resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss // 1024


def setup_env():
    # Cap the address space so the oversized allocations end in MemoryError
    # instead of the OOM killer.
    resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_AS, (3 << 30, 3 << 30))
    data = bomb_gif()
    im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(data))
    print(f"open(): {len(data)}-byte GIF, size={im.size}")
    return im


def poc(im):
    # An application skips the bomb frame and keeps going.
    try:
        im.seek(1)
    except Image.DecompressionBombError as e:
        print(f"seek(1) raised as intended: {e}")
        return True
    return False


im = setup_env()
raised = poc(im)

# Expected: a rejected frame leaves the object as it was (size == buffer == 1x1).
print(f"after the caught error: im.size={im.size}, pixel buffer im.im.size={im.im.size}")
poisoned = raised and im.size[0] * im.size[1] > LIMIT and im.im.size == (1, 1)

# Effect: retrying the seek lands on the real 1x1 frame, but load() sizes its
# buffers from the poisoned im.size.
before = peak_rss_mib()
im.seek(1)
try:
    im.load()
    outcome = "completed"
except MemoryError:
    outcome = "MemoryError at the 3 GiB cap"
after = peak_rss_mib()
print(f"seek(1) + load() of a 1x1 frame: {outcome}; peak RSS {before} MiB -> {after} MiB")
ballooned = after - before > 1000

print("BUG" if poisoned and ballooned else "OK")

References

  • https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/security/advisories/GHSA-65qm-jvmh-6pqg
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-112400
  • https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/commit/6faed707cfb760a4cbd726ddc8406f576cf35bf7
  • https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/releases/tag/13.0.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-65qm-jvmh-6pqg

entry.title: [Pillow] Pillow: EPS load(scale) lets Ghostscript render past the decompression bomb limit
entry.content:
============================================================================
EPS load(scale) lets Ghostscript render past the decompression bomb limit
Location: src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:92  in Ghostscript()
Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6
============================================================================

When an application opens an untrusted Encapsulated PostScript file and asks Pillow to render it at a larger scale, Pillow has Ghostscript produce an image several times bigger than Pillow's configured size limit allows. The size check runs only after Ghostscript has finished rendering and written the full raw image to a temporary file. An attacker who can upload a file of about 100 bytes makes each such request spend scale² times the Ghostscript rendering work and temporary disk space that the limit is meant to permit. For example, at scale 2 that is a 972 MB temporary file.

The cause is in Ghostscript() in src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py. It multiplies the file-declared size by the caller's scale (lines 93-94) and passes the product to gs as the -g output geometry. It never calls Image._decompression_bomb_check() on the scaled size. The only check is the one Image.open() ran on the unscaled size, so a file declaring 9000×9000 passes, and load(scale=2) then asks Ghostscript for 18000×18000 (3.6× MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS). A file declaring 18000×18000 directly would be refused before Ghostscript ever ran. DecompressionBombError fires only when Pillow reopens the output file, so Pillow's own in-process allocation stays bounded and there is no memory corruption.

The effect is a constant-factor overshoot rather than an unbounded one, for three reasons:

  • The multiplier is an integer chosen by the application, not by the file.
  • With the default warning filter, Image.open() already lets files up to 2× the limit reach Ghostscript at scale=1.
  • Any application feeding untrusted files to Ghostscript is already exposed to a tiny file that keeps Ghostscript busy indefinitely, since gs runs with no timeout.

This is the EPS counterpart of the WMF load(dpi) gap closed in af70b075a. It has been present since the decompression-bomb limit was introduced in ce2955ec7 (2.5.0). The attached reproducer stubs out Ghostscript and shows a 76-byte file passing Image.open() and reaching gs with -g18000x18000. A one-line patch mirroring the WMF check is included.

Details

EpsImageFile.load(scale=N) (the documented way to rasterise an EPS at higher resolution) renders width*N × height*N pixels through Ghostscript, but the only decompression-bomb check on the way is the one Image.open() ran on the unscaled, file-declared width × height. The scaled product is never passed to Image._decompression_bomb_check() before gs is started.

This 111-byte EPS declares 9000×9000 = 81,000,000 pixels, below the default MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS (89,478,485), so Image.open() accepts it without even a warning:

%!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0
%%BoundingBox: 0 0 9000 9000
%%EndComments
0 0 moveto 9000 9000 lineto stroke
showpage

im.load(scale=2) on it then executes

gs -q -g18000x18000 -r144.000000x144.000000 -dBATCH -dNOPAUSE -dSAFER -sDEVICE=pnmraw -sOutputFile=/tmp/tmpXXXX -c 0 0 translate -f attack.eps -c showpage

i.e. asks Ghostscript for an 18000×18000 = 324,000,000-pixel raster (3.6× MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS), whose pnmraw output is a 972,000,019-byte file in the temp directory. An EPS that declares 18000×18000 directly is rejected by Image.open() with DecompressionBombError before Ghostscript is ever run; via scale=2 the same raster is rendered first and the DecompressionBombError only appears afterwards, when Pillow opens the file Ghostscript produced. (Between 1× and 2× MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS, Image.open() only emits DecompressionBombWarning, so with the default warning filter an EPS declaring e.g. 13377×13377 is already rendered at scale=1 — a 537 MB PNM. Against that baseline, scale=2 is 4× an already-permitted render.)

The arithmetic is in Ghostscript():

# src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:91-97
    # Hack to support hi-res rendering
    scale = int(scale) or 1
    width = size[0] * scale
    height = size[1] * scale
    # resolution is dependent on bbox and size
    res_x = 72.0 * width / (bbox[2] - bbox[0])
    …
# src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:139-142
    command = [
        gs_binary,
        "-q",  # quiet mode
        f"-g{width:d}x{height:d}",  # set output geometry (pixels)
    …
# src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:165-168
        subprocess.check_call(command, startupinfo=startupinfo)
        with Image.open(outfile) as out_im:
            out_im.load()
            return out_im.im.copy()

and its caller does nothing between taking scale from the application and invoking it:

# src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:411-417
    def load(self, scale: int = 1, transparency: bool = False) -> …:
        # Load EPS via Ghostscript
        if self.tile:
            assert self.fp is not None
            self.im = Ghostscript(self.tile, self.size, self.fp, scale, transparency)

size here is self._size, computed in _open() from the file's %%BoundingBox (or %ImageData) and checked once by Image.open() at src/PIL/Image.py:3700. For the benign path (scale=1) that check covers exactly what Ghostscript is asked to render. For scale=N the rendered pixel count is N² times what was checked, so a file can sit just under the limit at open time and have Ghostscript render 4× (scale 2), 9× (scale 3), 16× (scale 4) the configured budget. The first point at which Pillow looks at the real size again is Image.open(outfile) at line 166 — after subprocess.check_call has returned, i.e. after Ghostscript has spent the CPU and written width*height*3 bytes to tempfile.mkstemp()'s directory.

WmfStubImageFile.load(dpi) has the same shape (file-derived extent × caller-supplied factor → new raster) and, since af70b075a, calls Image._decompression_bomb_check(self.size) on the recomputed size before rendering (src/PIL/WmfImagePlugin.py:127-131). The EPS path lacks the equivalent line. The gap dates from ce2955ec7128 ("Throw an exception when an opened image is larger than an arbitrary limit", 2014-05-14, first released in 2.5.0), which added the check to Image.open() without covering the scale path.

Impact

Affected are applications that open untrusted EPS/PS with Ghostscript installed and call load(scale=N) with a fixed N > 1, as the handbook suggests for non-blurry output. Handing untrusted EPS to Ghostscript at all already lets the same attacker tie up a worker with an equally tiny file (e.g. a PostScript {} loop; Pillow runs gs with no timeout), so this bug adds a constant factor rather than a new denial-of-service capability. Within that setting, a ~110-byte upload makes each request run Ghostscript over N² × MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS pixels (N² × 2·MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS if the application does not turn DecompressionBombWarning into an error) and write a W·H·3-byte PNM into the temp directory — 972 MB for the example above at scale 2, 2.2 GB at scale 3, 8.6 GB for a 178-Mpixel declaration at scale 4 — before any limit is applied. The operator's MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS setting is exceeded by a factor of N²; N is an integer chosen by the application, not by the file, so the work stays bounded at N² × 2·MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS. The consequence is N² more Ghostscript CPU and temp-disk use per request than the configured limit intends; Pillow's own in-process pixel allocation remains bounded because Image.open(outfile) re-checks the PNM's size, and there is no memory corruption.

This is a sibling of the WMF load(dpi) issue fixed in af70b075a ("Add decompression bomb check when loading at a different DPI"); the EPS scale path was not covered by that change. Unlike the WMF case, where the file-controlled _inch makes the ratio unbounded, the EPS multiplier is fixed by the application.

Reproducing

Run repro against the installed Pillow. Ghostscript does not need to be installed: the script sets EpsImagePlugin.gs_binary = "gs" so that has_ghostscript() skips its gs --version probe, and replaces subprocess.check_call with a function that records the command line Pillow builds and then raises OSError, so nothing is actually rendered.

It writes a 76-byte EPS declaring %%BoundingBox: 0 0 9000 9000 (the example above without the drawing line; 81 Mpixel, below the default MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS of 89,478,485) and turns DecompressionBombWarning into an error, so any bomb check — warning or hard error — counts. It then calls Image.open() and im.load(scale=2). Image.open() accepts the file and load(scale=2) reaches the intercepted Ghostscript call with -g18000x18000 (324,000,000 pixels, 3.6× MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS, a 972 MB pnmraw output with real Ghostscript). The script prints the geometry it captured.

It prints BUG when Ghostscript was invoked with a -g geometry above 2*MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS (178,956,970) and no decompression-bomb check fired before that call; otherwise it prints OK. With the attached patch applied, load(scale=2) raises DecompressionBombError before Ghostscript is called and the script prints OK.

Suggested fix

The attached patch checks the scaled size in Ghostscript() right after the scaled width/height are computed (src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:93-94) and before the gs command is built, mirroring WmfStubImageFile.load:

--- a/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py
+++ b/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py
@@ -92,6 +92,7 @@ def Ghostscript(
     scale = int(scale) or 1
     width = size[0] * scale
     height = size[1] * scale
+    Image._decompression_bomb_check((width, height))
     # resolution is dependent on bbox and size
     res_x = 72.0 * width / (bbox[2] - bbox[0])
     res_y = 72.0 * height / (bbox[3] - bbox[1])

load(scale=N) now raises DecompressionBombError / emits DecompressionBombWarning under the same MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS thresholds Image.open() applies, before Ghostscript runs instead of after. Placing the check in Ghostscript() rather than in EpsImageFile.load() is the single point where the rendered extent is decided, so it also covers direct callers of the module-level function. With the patch applied to a clean checkout the reproducer prints OK and Tests/test_file_eps.py passes. One cosmetic side effect: at scale=1 the check re-emits the DecompressionBombWarning that Image.open() already issued for sizes between 1× and 2× the limit; guarding the call with if scale > 1: would avoid the duplicate.

The patch also adds test_load_scale_decompression_bomb to Tests/test_file_eps.py, in the style of the WMF test: it sets MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS to im.width * im.height and expects im.load(scale=2) to raise DecompressionBombError. Like the rest of that file it is skipped without Ghostscript, because has_ghostscript() is consulted at the top of Ghostscript(); moving the check above that call would let the test run without it.

The patch

Add decompression bomb check on the scaled size in EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript() before Ghostscript is invoked

Applies to src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py at the commit above.

@@ -98,6 +98,14 @@ def test_sanity(filename: str, size: tuple[int, int], scale: int) -> None:

+    with Image.open(FILE1) as im:
+        monkeypatch.setattr(Image, "MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS", im.width * im.height)
+        with pytest.raises(Image.DecompressionBombError):
+            im.load(scale=2)
+
+

     with Image.open(FILE1) as im:

index 5eaefe339..ccc6f1d85 100644
--- a/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py

@@ -92,6 +92,7 @@ def Ghostscript(

The reproducer

Reproducer — repro, 1,845 bytes (click to open)

Its last line is BUG when the issue triggers and OK when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed BUG.

# unscaled WxH was checked by Image.open(). gs is not installed here, so we
# set gs_binary and intercept subprocess.check_call to read the argv Pillow builds.
import os, subprocess, tempfile, warnings
from PIL import Image, EpsImagePlugin

EpsImagePlugin.gs_binary = "gs"  # skip the `gs --version` probe
path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "a.eps")
with open(path, "w") as f:  # 9000x9000 = 81 Mpx < MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS (89.5 Mpx)
    f.write("%!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0\n%%BoundingBox: 0 0 9000 9000\n%%EndComments\nshowpage\n")

calls = []
def fake_check_call(cmd, **kw):
    calls.append(cmd)
    raise OSError("gs intercepted")  # stop here; we only need the argv
subprocess.check_call = fake_check_call

hard = 2 * Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS
bomb_before_gs = False
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("error", Image.DecompressionBombWarning)
    try:

            print("Image.open accepted", os.path.getsize(path), "byte EPS, size", im.size)
            im.load(scale=2)
    except (Image.DecompressionBombError, Image.DecompressionBombWarning) as e:
        bomb_before_gs = not calls

entry.title: [Pillow] Pillow: TiffDecode returns uninitialized memory as pixels for short JPEG strips
entry.content:
============================================================================
TiffDecode returns uninitialized memory as pixels for short JPEG strips
Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:554  in _decodeStrip()
Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6
============================================================================

Pillow hands back leftover process memory as image pixels when it opens a small crafted TIFF file. Anyone who can get an application to open their image, and can see something produced from its pixels (a thumbnail, a preview, a converted copy), can read heap memory that the process had previously used and freed. This works in the default configuration: opening and loading the 478-byte file succeeds with no error or warning, and every row below the first eight holds stale memory instead of picture content.

The bug is in _decodeStrip() in src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c, and _decodeTile() has the same shape. The function realloc()s state->buffer to TIFFStripSize() bytes without initialising it and calls TIFFReadEncodedStrip(). Whenever that call does not return -1, it copies all RowsPerStrip rows of the buffer into the image. libtiff's JPEG codec only warns when the JPEG embedded in a strip has fewer rows than the strip, and Pillow silences libtiff warnings. The codec decodes the rows that exist and still returns the full strip size, so the untouched remainder is copied out as pixels. libtiff's Group 4 fax codec behaves the same way for a stream that ends early.

The attached reproducer builds a 256×256 TIFF whose single strip or tile is a 256×8 JPEG. Before loading it, the script frees buffers filled with b"LEAK". It then finds 15,872 copies of LEAK in rows 8–255 of the decoded image (the same freed chunk was reused in 500 of 500 runs). Under glibc's MALLOC_PERTURB_, those rows are entirely the allocator's fill byte. A well-formed control file decodes correctly in both cases.

This is a read of uninitialised heap memory, not memory corruption. Each strip can disclose up to width × RowsPerStrip bytes, and what comes back depends on the allocator's state at the time. The strip path was introduced in e91b851fdc1c ("Add reading old-JPEG compressed TIFFs", first released in Pillow 6.0.0). The tile path has had the same pattern since f0436a4ddc95 (Pillow 5.3.0).

Details

src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c decodes compressed TIFFs through libtiff into a strip (or tile) buffer that it realloc()s to TIFFStripSize() bytes and never initialises, and then copies all RowsPerStrip rows of that buffer into the image whenever TIFFReadEncodedStrip() does not return -1. libtiff's JPEG codec does not fail when the JPEG stream inside a strip has fewer rows than the strip: it decodes the rows that exist and returns the full strip size. The rows it did not write are whatever the heap held before, and Pillow returns them as pixels.

A 478-byte file shows it: a classic little-endian TIFF, 256×256, BitsPerSample=8, Compression=7, PhotometricInterpretation=1, RowsPerStrip=256, one strip whose data is a baseline JPEG of 256×8 pixels (as written by Image.new("L",(256,8),200).save(…,"JPEG")). Image.open(BytesIO(data)).load() succeeds with default settings (compressed TIFFs always take the libtiff path). Rows 0–7 of the result are the JPEG content (value 200); the remaining 63488 bytes of im.tobytes() are heap garbage: run under glibc's MALLOC_PERTURB_=1 they are all 0xFE, under MALLOC_PERTURB_=170 all 0x55 (the fresh-malloc fill byte), and in a process that has just freed buffers containing b"LEAK" they contain 15872 copies of LEAK.

Feeding the same file to libtiff 4.5.0 directly confirms the library side: TIFFReadEncodedStrip(t, 0, buf, 65536) prints JPEGPreDecode: Warning, Improper JPEG strip/tile size, expected 256x256, got 256x8., returns 65536, and leaves 63488 of the 65536 buffer bytes untouched. Pillow installs TIFFSetWarningHandler(NULL) (TiffDecode.c:682), so the warning is not visible either.

The strip path:

// src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:552
    /* realloc to fit whole strip */
    /* malloc check above */
    new_data = realloc(state->buffer, state->bytes);      // state->bytes = TIFFStripSize()
    …
    state->buffer = new_data;

    for (; state->y < state->ysize; state->y += rows_per_strip) {
        …
            if (TIFFReadEncodedStrip(
                    tiff,
                    TIFFComputeStrip(tiff, state->y, plane),
                    (tdata_t)state->buffer,
                    strip_size
                ) == -1) {
                … return -1;
            }
            …
            // iterate over each row in the strip and stuff data into image
            for (strip_row = 0;
                 strip_row < MIN((INT32)rows_per_strip, state->ysize - state->y);
                 strip_row++) {
                …
                shuffler(
                    (UINT8 *)im->image[state->y + state->yoff + strip_row] +
                        state->xoff * im->pixelsize,
                    state->buffer + strip_row * row_byte_size,
                    state->xsize
                );

state->buffer arrives here as the one-row calloc made by decode.c:230 ((bits*xsize+7)/8 = 256 bytes for the example). The realloc to 65536 bytes hands back a different, uninitialised chunk; nothing zeroes it. TIFFReadEncodedStrip() returns the nominal strip size on success, not the number of rows produced, and the only check is == -1, so the row loop unconditionally copies 256 rows × 256 bytes into im->image (which itself is zeroed by core.new, so the garbage provably comes from state->buffer). _decodeTile() has the same shape (TiffDecode.c:448 realloc to TIFFTileSize(), then tile_length rows copied after each TIFFReadTile() at 460–488).

For a well-formed file the JPEG inside the strip is 256×256, libtiff fills all 65536 bytes and the copy is correct. The malicious file differs only in the SOF height of the embedded JPEG; libtiff treats "JPEG smaller than strip" as a warning, clamps the row count to the JPEG height, and reports success.

JPEG is not the only libtiff codec that succeeds on a short strip. Fax4Decode (Compression=4) returns success for a T.6 stream that ends early: a 133-byte 512×256 1-bit TIFF whose strip is the Group 4 stream of a 512×16 image loads without error, libtiff writes 17 rows (1088 bytes) of the 16384-byte buffer (Fax4Decode: Warning, Premature EOL at line 16, return value 16384) and the other 15296 bytes are again heap contents. LZW, Deflate, PackBits, Group 3 and CCITT RLE were checked and do return -1 on short data, so Pillow raises OSError for those.

The strip path was introduced in e91b851fdc1c ("Add reading old-JPEG compressed TIFFs", 2018-12-08), first released in Pillow 6.0.0, which replaced row-by-row TIFFReadScanline() (where libtiff errors on the first missing row) with the whole-strip realloc() and copy. The tile path has had the same shape since it was added in f0436a4ddc95 (2018-07-02, Pillow 5.3.0).

Impact

Any application that opens attacker-supplied images with Pillow in the default configuration and returns something derived from the pixels (thumbnail, preview, format conversion, OCR text) discloses freed heap memory of the worker process to the uploader: everything below the rows the embedded JPEG/G4 stream actually encodes, up to ImageWidth × RowsPerStrip × SamplesPerPixel bytes per strip and tens of MB per image within the default MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS. load() raises nothing, so the application has no signal that the image is malformed. What comes back depends on allocator state; in a long-running web worker it is typically recently freed request bodies, other users' decoded image buffers and Python object contents. There is no memory corruption; this is a read of uninitialised (previously used) heap memory, analogous in effect to an out-of-bounds read that lands in pixels.

Reproducing

repro is a short Python script that runs against the installed Pillow build with default settings: no rebuild, no sanitizer, no files written. It runs twice, once normally and once re-executing itself under glibc's MALLOC_PERTURB_=170, and the last line it prints is BUG or OK.

Input. tiff(jpeg_rows, tiled) builds a little-endian TIFF in memory. The header declares a 256×256 8-bit greyscale image with Compression=7 (JPEG), either as one strip (RowsPerStrip=256) or as one 256×256 tile (TileWidth/TileLength). The strip or tile is a baseline JPEG of 256×jpeg_rows pixels, all value 200, written by Pillow's own JPEG encoder. For each layout the script builds two files:

  • Control: jpeg_rows=256. This is a well-formed file, and libtiff fills the whole 64 KiB strip/tile.
  • Crafted: jpeg_rows=8, 478 bytes (strip) or 490 bytes (tile). The only difference is the embedded JPEG's height. libtiff decodes 8 rows (2048 bytes), warns Improper JPEG strip/tile size (Pillow silences the warning) and returns the full strip/tile size as success.

Steps. Each file is opened (the script asserts it takes the libtiff decoder). Just before im.load() the script allocates and frees six 64 KiB bytearrays filled with b"LEAK", which leaves freed heap chunks about the size of the buffer that _decodeStrip()/_decodeTile() is about to realloc(). For rows 8–255 it then counts copies of LEAK and bytes equal to 0x55 (glibc's fresh-malloc fill under MALLOC_PERTURB_=170). The files contain no LEAK bytes (the script asserts this), so any copy in the image came from freed heap memory. It reports BUG if a crafted file shows any LEAK in the normal pass, or rows 8–255 entirely 0x55 in the perturbed pass.

Expected output on this tree:

[normal ] strip well-formed (1222 B) rows 8-255:     0 x b'LEAK',     0/63488 == 0x55, head=b'\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8'
[normal ] strip crafted     ( 478 B) rows 8-255: 15872 x b'LEAK',     0/63488 == 0x55, head=b'LEAKLEAK'
[normal ] tiled well-formed (1234 B) rows 8-255:     0 x b'LEAK',     0/63488 == 0x55, head=b'\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8'
[normal ] tiled crafted     ( 490 B) rows 8-255: 15872 x b'LEAK',     0/63488 == 0x55, head=b'LEAKLEAK'
[perturb] strip well-formed (1222 B) rows 8-255:     0 x b'LEAK',     0/63488 == 0x55, head=b'\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8'
[perturb] strip crafted     ( 478 B) rows 8-255:     0 x b'LEAK', 63488/63488 == 0x55, head=b'UUUUUUUU'
[perturb] tiled well-formed (1234 B) rows 8-255:     0 x b'LEAK',     0/63488 == 0x55, head=b'\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8\xc8'
[perturb] tiled crafted     ( 490 B) rows 8-255:     0 x b'LEAK', 63488/63488 == 0x55, head=b'UUUUUUUU'
BUG

im.load() succeeds for every file. For the crafted files rows 8–255 are the uninitialised strip/tile buffer, copied as-is into the image. With the attached patch applied, rows 8–255 of the crafted files come back as \x00 bytes, with no LEAK and no 0x55, and the script ends with OK.

The LEAK count depends on where glibc places the buffer (the same freed chunk was reused in 500 of 500 runs here); the MALLOC_PERTURB_ pass does not. The script covers the JPEG codec only. The Group 4 variant in the Details section (Compression=4, a T.6 stream that ends early) goes through the same _decodeStrip() copy, and the same fix covers it.

Suggested fix

The attached patch zeroes state->buffer before each libtiff read in both loops of src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c — before TIFFReadTile() in _decodeTile() and before TIFFReadEncodedStrip() in _decodeStrip() — so rows a codec does not produce are deterministic zeros rather than stale heap:

--- a/src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c
+++ b/src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c
@@ _decodeTile
             for (x = state->xoff; x < state->xsize; x += tile_width) {
+                memset(state->buffer, 0, state->bytes);
                 if (TIFFReadTile(tiff, (tdata_t)state->buffer, x, y, 0, plane) == -1) {
@@ _decodeStrip
         for (plane = 0; plane < planes; plane++) {
             ImagingShuffler shuffler = unpackers[plane];
+            memset(state->buffer, 0, state->bytes);
             if (TIFFReadEncodedStrip(

A memset per strip/tile (rather than one calloc after the size is known) is needed because the same buffer is reused for every strip, and a short last strip would otherwise expose the previous strip's rows — harmless for disclosure, but the per-read memset keeps the behaviour uniform at the cost of one extra pass over the buffer. Promoting libtiff warnings to errors via a warning handler is not a good alternative: both codecs only warn (Improper JPEG strip/tile size, Premature EOL), but so do many legitimate files (unknown tags, bad tag counts), and the return value of TIFFReadEncodedStrip() carries no row count to check against. Initialising the buffer covers every codec. _decodeAsRGBA() needs no change: TIFFRGBAImageGet() fills its whole raster, and JPEG files do not reach it (JPEGCOLORMODE_RGB sends them down the strip path).

Valid files decode exactly as before; rows a codec does not produce are now black instead of garbage, and nothing that previously loaded now fails. The patch also adds test_jpeg_short_strip to Tests/test_file_libtiff.py, parametrised over strip and tile, which builds the 256×8-JPEG-in-256×256 file and asserts rows 8–255 are zero. It is a regression guard for the fixed code rather than a reliable detector of the bug: in a fresh pytest process the unfixed strip variant can pass because the new heap chunk happens to be zero (the tiled variant fails before the fix). With the patch, Tests/test_file_libtiff.py and Tests/test_file_tiff.py pass and the reproducer prints OK.

The patch

Zero the libtiff strip/tile buffer before each TIFFReadEncodedStrip/TIFFReadTile in TiffDecode.c so short strips do not expose uninitialised heap

Applies to src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c at the commit above.

--- a/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py

The reproducer

Reproducer — repro, 2,688 bytes (click to open)

Its last line is BUG when the issue triggers and OK when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed BUG.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# Pillow TiffDecode.c _decodeStrip/_decodeTile: strip/tile buffer is realloc()ed, never
# initialised, and copied whole into the image even when libtiff's JPEG codec decoded
# fewer rows than RowsPerStrip/TileLength.  Two independent signals:
#  pass 1 (normal heap): seed freed 64 KiB chunks with b"LEAK" just before load() and
#         count copies of LEAK in the decoded pixels (file contains no such bytes);
#  pass 2 (same script re-run under glibc MALLOC_PERTURB_=170): fresh malloc memory is
#         0x55, so rows that come back all-0x55 are provably uninitialised heap.
import gc, io, os, struct, subprocess, sys
from PIL import Image
W = H = 256; ROWS = 8
perturbed = os.environ.get("MALLOC_PERTURB_") == "170"
if not perturbed:
    print("Pillow", Image.__version__, Image.core.__file__)

def tiff(jpeg_rows, tiled):
    j = io.BytesIO(); Image.new("L", (W, jpeg_rows), 200).save(j, "JPEG"); j = j.getvalue()
    tags = [(256,3,1,W), (257,3,1,H), (258,3,1,8), (259,3,1,7), (262,3,1,1), (277,3,1,1)]
    tags += ([(322,3,1,W), (323,3,1,H), (324,4,1,0), (325,4,1,len(j))] if tiled else
             [(273,4,1,0), (278,3,1,H), (279,4,1,len(j))])
    tags.sort(); off = 8 + 2 + 12*len(tags) + 4
    tags = [(t,ty,c, off if t in (273,324) else v) for t,ty,c,v in tags]
    ifd = struct.pack("<H", len(tags)) + b"".join(struct.pack("<HHLL", *t) for t in tags)
    return b"II*\0" + struct.pack("<L", 8) + ifd + struct.pack("<L", 0) + j

bug = False
for tiled in (False, True):
    for jpeg_rows, label in ((H, "well-formed"), (ROWS, "crafted")):
        data = tiff(jpeg_rows, tiled); assert b"LEAK" not in data
        im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(data)); assert im.tile[0][0] == "libtiff"
        junk = [bytearray(b"LEAK" * (W*H//4)) for _ in range(6)]; del junk; gc.collect()
        im.load()                                   # no exception for either file
        below = im.tobytes()[W*ROWS:]
        n55, nleak = below.count(0x55), below.count(b"LEAK")
        print(f"[{'perturb' if perturbed else 'normal '}] {'tiled' if tiled else 'strip'} "
              f"{label:11s} ({len(data):4d} B) rows {ROWS}-{H-1}: {nleak:5d} x b'LEAK', "
              f"{n55:5d}/{len(below)} == 0x55, head={below[:8]!r}")
        if jpeg_rows == ROWS and (nleak > 0 or (perturbed and n55 == len(below))):
            bug = True
if not perturbed:
    r = subprocess.run([sys.executable, sys.argv[0]], env={**os.environ, "MALLOC_PERTURB_": "170"},
                       capture_output=True, text=True)
    lines = r.stdout.rstrip().split("\n")
    print("\n".join(lines[:-1])); sys.stderr.write(r.stderr)
    bug = bug or lines[-1] == "BUG"
print("BUG" if bug else "OK")
